title: Direct and plant‐mediated responses in microbial resource limitation under simulated global change in alpine steppe soils
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Soil microorganisms play a fundamental role in terrestrial carbon (C) and nutrient cycling. Their metabolic rates are limited by the resource in the shortest supply. Altered precipitation and warming-accelerated nutrient cycling are expected to modify plant-derived C inputs and soil nitrogen (N) availability, redefining the resource landscape for microbial growth. Here, we conducted a two-year field experiment in an alpine steppe on the Tibetan Plateau to assess how altered precipitation and N enrichment affected microbial resource availability. Precipitation treatments included ambient, −50% and +50%, whereas N treatments included ambient N and annual N additions at moderate (+10 g N m−2) and extreme (+40 g N m−2) levels. To assess microbial resource limitations, we used a limiting factor assay (LFA) to determine instantaneous growth responses to factorial additions of C, N and phosphorus (P). We found that moderate N stimulated above-ground productivity, whereas extreme N suppressed it. Drought markedly reduced above-ground productivity, with only marginal gains under increased precipitation. Microbial growth was primarily limited by C across all treatments, but the strength of C limitation declined in treatments with higher above-ground productivity. Consequently, moderate N alleviated microbial C limitation, with microbial growth stimulation by C-containing LFA additions ca. 200–400 percentage points lower than under ambient N. Neither extreme N nor altered precipitation alleviated microbial C limitation. N treatments enhanced microbial C use efficiency, while altered precipitation treatments accelerated microbial turnover. Moderate N also increased the fungal-to-bacterial growth ratio in response to LFA additions, but this effect was attenuated under increased precipitation, which also enhanced bacterial richness and favoured moisture-responsive taxa. Our findings highlight an above-ground–below-ground linkage through which environmental change shapes microbial C limitation via changes in the plant-derived C supply, with implications for microbial C processing and soil C persistence in resource-poor alpine steppes.
